Making yogurt in a slow cooker
- Monitor temperature: using a thermometer is highly recommended when heating milk for yogurt. Heating to the proper range is important for killing unwanted bacteria and preparing the milk for cultures — it’s more reliable than simply waiting a set time.  
- Follow a tested slow-cooker yogurt recipe for milk volume, starter amount, and incubation time (you asked about heating for 2–3 hours; a thermometer removes uncertainty).  

Cashew-based (vegan) yogurt tips
- Soak well: rinse 1 cup cashews and soak them at least 4 hours or overnight to rehydrate and make them easy to blend.  
- Drain and rinse after soaking.  
- Blend: add the soaked cashews to a high-speed blender with about 1/2 cup fresh water (adjust for desired thickness) and blend on high until very smooth and creamy (about ~2 minutes in our notes).  
- Strain/finish: after blending, strain or smooth as needed to reach the texture you like, then proceed with your yogurt-culturing method or add your vegan starter/cultures.  

Flavoring and sweetening ideas
- Vanilla, cinnamon, and fresh fruit were suggested as straightforward ways to flavor slow-cooker yogurt. You can also add sweeteners like maple syrup or honey (or plant-based sweeteners for vegan yogurt).

Great — here are some store-shopping tips based on what you’ve already discussed about Les Pauls, open tunings, and guitar setup:

- Try different body types and constructions: bolt-on (Strat) vs set neck (Les Paul) and how the guitar’s body wood and shape feel and sound to you. These affect tone and comfort.
- Check pickups and tonal options: humbuckers (thicker, fuller tone) vs single-coils. If you want more tonal flexibility, try guitars with coil-tap/coil-splitting to get brighter single-coil-like tones from humbuckers.
- Playability and neck feel: test neck profiles and fretboard feel for comfort — what’s good for one player may be fatiguing for another.
- String gauge and tuning needs: if you plan lower or alternate tunings (like open D), try heavier strings and see how the guitar handles lower tension; heavier strings give fuller tone in lower tunings.
- Setup and action: play guitars unplugged and amplified to judge action, buzzing, and intonation. A well-set-up instrument will feel and sound better; ask if the store can adjust action or intonation before you decide.
- Try the styles you play: if you want to fingerpick or get acoustic-like tones, test how the electric responds to light picking (some models with humbuckers can be thicker and less “acoustic” sounding).
- Amp and EQ test: plug into an amp and try different amp settings to hear how the guitar’s pickups interact with gain, tone, and your typical playing style.
- Comfort and ergonomics: sit/stand and play for several minutes to check weight, balance, and how it feels for chord work and lead lines.
- Ask about returns/setup service and upgrades: batteryless warranties, setups, and whether features (like coil-splits) are factory or aftermarket.

Bring ideas of the tunings/styles you’ll use (e.g., open D, fingerpicking, rock) so you can test guitars with those in mind. Have fun at the store this weekend!
